lede: In one night, models from two labs played 29 games of real Factorio through screenshots, mouse and keyboard: alone, in teams sharing a factory, and as rival teams on one map. The game's own server kept the score. The set-up works, it produces clear differences between models, and the first results on teamwork and competition are below.
headlines:
• It is possible, and cheap enough to iterate on. 25 of 29 games ran the full 20 game minutes, 9,887 model turns in all, for $312.01. No GPU, no game modding beyond a scenario file of under 100 lines, and no model touched the game's console.
  • Models differ a lot at playing alone. GPT-6.2 Astra scored 25,021, GPT-6.2 Sol 18,785, Claude Fable 5.2 18,617, Claude Opus 5.5 6,736 (mean of 4), Claude Sonnet 5.5 1,370 and Claude Haiku 5.5 932.
  • Teams out-produce individuals, with sharply falling returns. Two Claude Opus 5.5 agents averaged 1.8 times one agent's score; four averaged 2.1 times. Per agent, a team of four produced about half what an agent produces alone.
  • Competition for land changed the outcome. With four models on one map, Astra scored 26,135, about what it scores alone, while Fable fell from 18,617 alone to 4,294 and Opus from 6,736 to 3,277. Astra covered the coal field with drills early and the others ran short of fuel.
  • Written notes mostly did not help. Models played alone starting from the notes Fable wrote after its own game: Opus 5.5 went from 6,736 to 7,833; Sonnet 5.5 went from 1,370 to 3,094; Haiku 5.5 went from 932 to 887; Fable 5.2 went from 18,617 to 16,618. Four generations of Opus teams passing notes down showed no upward trend either.
  • The measurements are noisy. Identical two-agent games scored between 7,679 and 21,163. Most conditions here were played once, so treat single comparisons as leads, not findings.
solo: Each model played the same 20-minute game alone on the same map. The gap is mostly in how much each one built. Astra placed 67 mining drills and 32 furnaces in 20 minutes; Opus placed 13 and 6. The two GPT models work in many small steps (over 500 turns each), while Fable got a similar score to Sol in about 150 turns by sending long batches of actions. Cost per game ran from $0.24 (Haiku) to $24.08 (Astra).
teams: The same model, Claude Opus 5.5, played alone, as a team of two and as a team of four, sharing one factory and one score, on two different maps. One agent averaged 6,736, two averaged 12,344 and four averaged 13,842. The second agent roughly doubled output; the third and fourth added little. Teams did organise themselves without being told to: in every team game the agents split the map by resource in the first minute and carried fuel and materials to each other. They sent about 20 chat messages per game.

versus: Four models were put on one map, each on its own team with its own buildings and score, sharing the same ore fields. Nothing stopped them interfering with each other except a cease-fire on weapons. Astra finished with 26,135, 6 times the next team. The Claude models scored far below what they score alone on the same map. Their own reasoning says why: Astra's drills occupied the coal field, coal is the fuel for everything else at this stage, and the others spent their time walking around someone else's machines. No team sent a message to another team in any game.

two_v_two: An earlier match, Claude Opus 5.5 against GPT-6.2 Astra, stood at 16,561 to 2,665 for Astra when it ended early at 15:50: an Opus agent clicked Quit in the game's menu, which at that point ended the game for everyone. The harness now puts such a player back in.
notes: At the end of each game every agent was asked for the notes it would leave the next player. Two tests used them. In the first, four generations of two-agent Opus teams each started from the previous team's notes. Scores went 21,163, 12,384, 11,728, 13,807: no upward trend, and the first team, with no notes, happened to be the best. In the second, models played alone starting from the notes Fable wrote after its solo game. Only Sonnet did clearly better with them; Fable's notes are specific and correct, but most of what separates the models here seems to be execution through the screen, which notes do not transfer.

org: Four Opus agents played the same game three ways: with no structure, with the first agent named as manager, and with four roles assigned in advance. Unstructured teams scored 14,960 and 14,360. The managed team scored 12,792. The manager did manage: it posted a plan in the first seconds, sent each agent to a resource, and the others acknowledged and reported back, but the result was no better. One game per structure is not enough to rank them.
distrust:
• Few games per condition. Only Opus alone (4 games), Opus pairs (4) and Opus fours (3) were repeated. Every other number on this page is one game.
  • Twenty minutes is the early game. Nobody got past burner drills and stone furnaces. At this horizon the score mostly rewards digging and hand-crafting, and Astra's winning play (self-fuelling coal drills, then crafting chests for points) would not be the best play in a longer game.
  • Spending differs between models. Astra took about three times as many turns as Fable and cost twice as much per game. Everything ran at medium reasoning effort; nothing was tuned per model.
  • The machines were overloaded. Five game clients shared four CPU cores with software rendering, at 5 to 8 frames a second. To save CPU the clients are briefly frozen while models think, which sometimes puts the game's "player is being dropped" warning on other players' screens.
  • The Quit button. Agents quit the game by accident through the Escape menu five times (Opus four times, Fable once). Three games ended early before the harness learned to put the player back in; they are listed under Every game and left out of the charts. A fourth game could not start because the game before it left no notes.
  • One model family per team. No mixed-lab teams were tried, and the map was the same in all but three games.
next:
• Repeat everything five times. At $5 to $25 a game, a real leaderboard with error bars is a few hundred dollars.
  • Longer games on a GPU machine. One to three game hours reaches electricity, research and automation, where organisation should matter far more than it does when everyone is digging by hand.
  • Real conflict. The harness already has a switch that lets teams attack each other, and the game ships its own team modes. The interesting version is the one where what you produce hurts the other side.
  • More agents per team. Four was the limit of one small machine, not of the design.
  • A rating. With repeats, the matches give a single head-to-head rating per model, as in the Clocktower benchmark.
method:
• The models play the real game by hand. Each agent has its own copy of Factorio 2.1 on its own virtual screen. It sees screenshots and acts with the mouse and keyboard. Claude and GPT models get exactly the same set of actions.
  • The clock only runs while someone is acting. The game is paused whenever any agent is thinking. Every agent acts at its own pace, and an agent in the middle of a long action is frozen through each pause.
  • The score is the game's own. It is the production score from Factorio's PvP mode: the value, at the game's price list, of everything a team has produced and not used up. Wood and fish count for nothing, and science spent on research keeps its value.
  • The game closes off cheating. Agents are ordinary players, not admins, so the game refuses console commands and logs each attempt. There were none.
  • One start, one deadline. Standard freeplay, fixed map, standard starting items, peaceful natives, permanent daylight, 20 game minutes.
